{{Short description|Chinese philosophical concept}}
{{Epistemology sidebar}}
The '''unity of knowledge and action''' (Chinese: 知行合一) is a concept in philosophy created by [[Wang Shouren|Wang Yangming]]. It means that knowledge and action should go together and help each other. This idea says that only by behaving well can someone become wise.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Wang Yangming (Wang Shou-Jen) {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/wangyang/|access-date=2023-04-01|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Overview ==
In Chinese philosophy, knowledge and action were traditionally seen as related but distinct. Wang argued there was no difference between them. He thought that knowledge was knowing how to act in a situation, based on his ideas about people and their innate knowledge. He also believed that the world was always changing, rather than staying the same.<ref name=":1" />

== History ==
[[Wang Shouren|Wang Yangming]] developed the concept during the [[Ming dynasty]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://sunypress.edu/Books/T/The-Unity-of-Knowledge-and-Action|title=The Unity of Knowledge and Action}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Lv|first1=Xianli|last2=Wu|first2=Zhongxue|date=June 2018|title=The philosophy of 'unity of knowledge and action' in interventional neuroradiology teaching|journal=The Neuroradiology Journal|volume=31|issue=3|pages=330–332|doi=10.1177/1971400917707350|issn=1971-4009|pmc=5958493|pmid=28660798}}</ref> in response to a disagreement with the teachings of [[Zhu Xi]].

Wang Yangming disagreed with the teachings of [[Zhu Xi]]. Zhu Xi encouraged students to study in two parts, one theoretical and one practical. Wang believed this approach made people ineffective.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web| title=What Is the “Unity” in the “Unity of Knowledge and Action”? | author=Harvey Lederman | date=2022-09-03 | url=https://philpapers.org/archive/LEDWIT.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230104230815/https://philpapers.org/archive/LEDWIT.pdf | archive-date=2023-01-04}}</ref>

== Application ==
Western philosophers talk about ''[[akrasia]]'', which is when someone does something they know is wrong on purpose. But Wang disagrees. He says that just saying you know something is wrong isn't enough. You have to actually act on what you know for it to count. For example, if a student cheats on a test but says cheating is wrong, Wang would say they don't really understand what they're saying.<ref name=":3">{{Citation|last=Van Norden|first=Bryan|title=Wang Yangming|date=2022|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2022/entries/wang-yangming/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2022|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2023-04-07|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>
